question: Papilloedema on fundoscopy is an absolute contraindication to lumbar puncture, as performing LP in this context risks fatal brainstem herniation.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is true. Papilloedema = raised ICP = absolute contraindication to LP. Removing CSF via lumbar puncture when ICP is raised creates a sudden pressure gradient that can force the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum (brainstem herniation) — a neurosurgical emergency with high mortality. If raised ICP is suspected (papilloedema, focal neurological signs, deteriorating consciousness), perform a CT scan first before any LP. Never rush LP in a child with these features.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure. Performing lumbar puncture when ICP is elevated risks transtentorial or cerebellar tonsillar herniation — a potentially fatal complication as the brainstem is compressed by the pressure gradient created by removing CSF. Other contraindications to LP include focal neurological signs, altered level of consciousness, and suspected spinal cord compression. The correct sequence when raised ICP is suspected: stabilise, perform neuroimaging first, and only proceed to LP when safe.
